Kho5KvPBDSw.summary: Confirmation bias makes us seek, interpret and remember information that fits what we already believe, which is useful for quick decisions but can be reduced by slowing down and reflecting.

points.text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to look for, interpret and remember information in ways that support what we already believe.
We view objective facts through the lens of our own beliefs, so we overrate evidence that fits them.
The bias is strongest on emotionally charged issues or when we are searching for a result we want.
Confirmation bias is often passed down through generations via stories, cultural beliefs and family values, such as the priest's and the atheist's upbringings.
In new situations, bias helps us reach quick conclusions, because weighing every possible outcome would be too costly and we would never decide.
To survive in a dangerous world, humans became storytelling, pattern-seeking animals, each convinced their own story is the right one.
Slowing down and thinking deeply lets us become aware of our biases and see that things are more complicated than we thought.
Repetition can make falsehoods believable because familiarity is hard to tell apart from truth, so reflecting when there is time is a good idea.

iKU6hhJM0-A.summary: Critical thinking means cutting through the extras to reach a topic's core concept, viewing it from several angles, and connecting different subjects instead of studying them separately.

points.text: Critical thinking means going straight to the core concept of anything you hear, asking what the basic idea is and what is really being said.
Aim to reach a concept so clearly that you could explain it simply, as if to a five-year-old.
Many things sound complex when described, but a good teacher shows they are actually simple. The difficulty often comes from extra detail around the basics.
To think critically, strip away the extra material around a topic so that only the basic concepts remain.
Don't rely on one source. Look at the same topic on YouTube, in other talks, and in texts to see different angles.
Seeing the same thing from different angles automatically increases your critical thinking.
Every field is connected to the others, even though we usually treat subjects like geography, history and languages as separate.
Find how different subjects link together and build your thinking from those links.
Link what you learn across subjects. For example, Newton's work on gravity happened in the same period as events in French history, so they can be studied together.
When you study history alongside science and maths, everything becomes one single subject, which develops critical thinking.

DxcBdFZPXaQ.summary: Logic is a philosopher's tool for building and checking arguments, which are premises leading to a conclusion, and it separates valid from invalid and deductive from inductive reasoning.

points.text: Logic is like a weapon in a philosopher's toolkit. The philosopher's job is to ask questions, form premises and build arguments.
The word 'logic' comes from the Greek word 'logos', which has two meanings, one of them being 'word'.
Logic lets you tell good arguments from bad ones. It works as a bridge that shows the difference between valid and invalid.
Every argument has two parts: the premises and the conclusion.
A premise is the backbone you give before explaining a claim. The conclusion is the claim itself, such as 'it rained today'.
Arguments are of two kinds: deductive and inductive.
In a deductive argument, if the premises are true, the conclusion has to be true.
A deductive conclusion can be false only if at least one premise is false, so you cannot make a mistake with true premises.
A deductive argument works from its form alone, so you don't need to know what the terms mean. 'A is B, B is D, so A is D' is enough.
In an inductive argument, true premises do not guarantee a true conclusion, so the conclusion may or may not be true.

tSuOtpSlTqs.summary: Brain rot happens because social media exploits primitive brain systems like a slot machine, but it can be fixed by adding friction, cutting screen time, and making your brain put in effort.

points.text: Brain rot is losing lots of time scrolling without noticing. It is a fixable neurological problem, not a moral failing or your fault.
Dopamine is the brain chemical that gives happiness from rewards, and it spikes more when rewards are unpredictable, sometimes coming and sometimes not.
Scrolling works like a casino slot machine: you never know if the next reel will be fun or scary, so the uncertainty keeps your brain excited and scrolling.
The old limbic brain chases instant rewards, while the prefrontal cortex plans long-term and controls it. When you are tired or stressed, the prefrontal cortex weakens and scrolling rises.
Add friction between you and your phone, especially after waking up. Scrolling right away raises cortisol and disrupts dopamine, so keep the phone away for the first 30 minutes.
Grey scale mode removes colors designed to hook attention, making the phone black and white so your interest in opening certain apps drops.
Do a weekly audit: check your screen time and turn it into a competitive game, trying to lower your weekly average by at least 30 minutes.

dItUGF8GdTw.summary: Critical thinking is a skeptical, five-step process (question, gather, apply, consider implications, explore other views) that helps you sift information and make better decisions.

points.text: Critical thinking is a way of carefully breaking down a situation to reveal hidden issues like bias and manipulation, so you can make the best decision.
A critical thinker doesn't pick what feels right; they test all options with skepticism and keep only the most useful, reliable information.
Step one: formulate your question. Know clearly what you want, so distracting claims don't hide your real goal.
Step two: gather information. A clear question tells you which of the many available sources are relevant, such as experts or other people's testimonies.
Step three: apply the information by asking critical questions about the concepts at work, your assumptions, and whether your reasoning is logically sound.
Testing assumptions against evidence exposes weak claims, such as assuming a sender promising millions is honest when the evidence doesn't make winning logical.
Step four: consider the implications. A choice that looks good at first may have unintended long-term consequences, like cheaper gas causing more air pollution.
Step five: explore other points of view, even opposing ones, to understand why others find certain policies appealing.
Looking at other viewpoints lets you explore alternatives and evaluate your own choices, leading to more informed decisions.
The five steps are just one tool; they won't remove hard decisions but can raise the number of good choices you make.

Qt4f7QrfRRc.summary: A slippery slope argument claims one step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome, but it overstates the likelihood, since real events form a web of possibilities, not a chain.

points.text: A slippery slope argument says one step (A) sets off a chain of events that inevitably ends in an extreme outcome (Z).
Slippery slopes can lead to extreme good outcomes as well as catastrophes; the slope is just as slippery either way.
Presenting Z as the certain result of A almost always overstates how likely Z is if A happens.
Each extra step adds a chance for the outcome to change, so even steps that are 99% likely leave A only about 78% likely to lead to Z.
Lowering the odds per step shrinks the overall chance fast: 95% per step gives about 28%, and 90% per step gives only 7%.
One weak link matters a lot: a single 50% step among 99% steps cuts the chance of reaching Z from 78% to 39%.
Real-world events are not like dominoes, where one falling guarantees the last falls; each event has many possible outcomes affecting the others, forming a web, not a chain.
In the Vietnam example, the first step happened but the predicted end result did not, and many steps in between never occurred.
Slippery slope arguments focus only on extreme outcomes with false certainty, distracting from more likely possibilities and shutting down more productive discussion.
People can deliberately use slippery slope arguments to exploit fears, since it is easy to invent an extreme outcome that suits any position.

vNDYUlxNIAA.summary: The Socratic Method uses probing questions, not lectures or answers, to expose hidden assumptions and flawed logic, helping people reach clearer understanding in many fields.

points.text: Socrates engaged people in long conversations about morality and society, responding to their answers only with further questions rather than lecturing or giving advice.
By questioning, Socrates probed people's logic, exposed its flaws, and helped both people reach a stronger understanding.
In the Euthydemus dialogue, each confident answer about justice met a new example that broke it, showing the young man he did not fully understand justice.
Socrates called himself a midwife because his questions help others give birth to their own ideas.
The method draws out unexamined assumptions and challenges biases, clarifying questions and removing contradictory or circular logic, even if it gives no final answer.
Following a line of inquiry wherever logic leads can take both the asker and answerer to unexpected conclusions.
Because it does not depend on the topic, the method has been used in medicine, sciences, faith questions, and law, including today's Supreme Court reasoning about a law's unintended impacts.
Law teachers use the method by challenging students with unforeseen hypothetical situations to test their understanding of judicial reasoning.
An effective Socratic teacher knows the subject well and is modest, curious, and affirming, rather than bullying students or showing off intelligence.

Ghbkv0MKV-w.summary: The conjunction fallacy is wrongly judging a story with more conditions as more likely because it seems plausible, though extra conditions always make an event less probable.

points.text: Most people pick 'artist who plays poker' over 'artist' for Lucy, because her math background fits poker. This choice is wrong.
The plain statement is more likely because it is less specific. It makes no claims about what else Lucy does.
A statement with two parts is true only if both parts are true, so adding a condition makes it less likely.
The chance of A happening is always greater than the chance of A and B both happening.
Picture a million math majors: everyone who is an artist and plays poker is also an artist, but not the reverse. The bigger group is the artists.
The conjunction fallacy is judging a statement with more conditions as more believable, even though more conditions make it less likely.
Under time pressure we use shortcuts, choosing what seems plausible and representative over what is statistically most probable.
Extra detail creates a narrative that fits our intuitions, so the option feels more plausible. Even people who understand statistics fall for this.
Conspiracy theories and false news use this fallacy, piling on resonant details so an outlandish story seems more believable.
A story can never be more likely to be true than its least likely component.

OGbE3wLmNzA.summary: Your brain uses mental shortcuts called cognitive biases that mislead your decisions, and you can counter three big ones (sunk cost, confirmation, availability) plus Dunning-Kruger by questioning your own thinking.

points.text: Cognitive biases are brain shortcuts that once helped survival but now mislead everyday decisions, so feeling stuck is often bias, not weak willpower or discipline.
The sunk cost fallacy is judging future decisions by what you already invested, like staying in a disliked job or bad relationship because you put in years.
Confirmation bias means your brain looks for evidence that supports what you already believe and ignores evidence that challenges it.
To counter confirmation bias, when you feel sure, deliberately write the opposite argument, find five points that break your belief, and then decide.
The availability heuristic makes you treat things that come easily to memory as more important or likely, even when they are rare, like plane crashes versus car accidents.
To counter the availability heuristic, when you feel very afraid or hopeful, ask what the real data says and whether you are generalizing from rare examples.
The Dunning-Kruger effect: beginners overestimate their ability, while experts underestimate theirs because they know how much can go wrong.
To counter Dunning-Kruger, if you feel very confident without experience, pause, research and talk to an expert; an expert's self-doubt is maturity, not impostor syndrome.
Build a nightly habit: write one important decision, why you are making it, and which bias (confirmation, availability or Dunning-Kruger) may be coloring it.

IKx7SJkDa2I.summary: The brain makes predictable thinking errors, such as overconfidence, following crowds, and believing repeated claims, but recognizing these seven mental traps helps you make better decisions.

points.text: Overconfidence effect: trusting your knowledge or judgment too much makes you ignore risk and become careless, like skipping seat belts or helmets, as with the Titanic's crew.
Conformity effect: when people around you hold an opinion, you start changing your own view to match theirs, even against what your own eyes see.
In the line-matching experiment, a person gave the wrong answer because everyone else did. Unanimous voices make the brain doubt its own judgment and treat majority opinion as truth.
Illusory truth effect: a claim heard again and again starts to feel true because it becomes familiar, even though repetition does not make it true.
Judge a claim by the solid evidence behind it, not by how often you have seen it or how many people repeat it.
Sunk cost fallacy: after investing time, money or effort, you stay in a bad choice to protect that loss, even though the lost investment never comes back.
Confirmation bias: once you believe something, you notice only evidence supporting it and ignore or explain away evidence against it.
Before each decision, ask yourself whether you are seeing the truth or your mind is fooling you. This question helps you catch these traps.

FG_VWStchdk.summary: The mind has a fast automatic thinking mode and a slow careful one, and many bad choices come from biases like rushing, missing information, loss fear, anchors and memory.

points.text: The mind has two ways of thinking: System 1 is fast, automatic and habit-based, while System 2 is slow and careful.
System 2 thinks slowly, needs focus and uses a lot of energy, like when you first learn to drive.
With practice, tasks that once needed System 2 become automatic and move to System 1, which saves brain energy.
Do not rush big decisions about money, career or relationships. Sleep on it so System 2 can think clearly.
WYSIATI (What You See Is All There Is): the brain treats the information in front of it as the whole story and ignores what is missing.
To beat WYSIATI, pause and ask what you are not being told, and look for the hidden facts.
Loss aversion: losing something hurts about twice as much as gaining the same thing feels good. This is the core of prospect theory.
The sunk cost fallacy is clinging to money, time or effort already spent. Judge a choice by the future, for example by asking if you would start this again today.
The anchoring effect: the first number or information you get becomes a starting point, and later thinking circles around it, even if it is irrelevant.
The peak-end rule: the remembering self judges an experience mostly by its most intense moment (peak) and by how it ended, not by its whole length.

d2r7Bk1NlgU.summary: Our brains use mental shortcuts that create unconscious cognitive biases, and scientific thinking, with evidence, community checking, and bias-reducing methods, helps us overcome them.

points.text: Cognitive biases are predictable weaknesses in how we evolved to think, and they lead us astray when we trust intuition alone on big, complex questions.
Heuristics are mental shortcuts built on pattern recognition. They copy old stories onto new information so we solve simple problems quickly without spending lots of brain power.
Cognitive biases are unconscious, implicit influences on decisions, unlike explicit bias, and everyone has them. They are not inherently bad.
Confirmation bias is accepting information that agrees with what we already believe and filtering out what contradicts it. It helps myths like learning styles persist.
Randomized controlled trials reduce bias by choosing participants at random and comparing a treatment group against a control group that gets a placebo, no treatment, or an older proven drug.
Double-blind studies reduce bias further because neither the participants nor the scientists know who is in the trial group and who is in the control group.
You can fight your own biases by accepting that you have them, and by interacting with many different people, since bias tells us our experience is the only reality.
Cognitive flexibility is the ability to imagine options or explanations beyond your gut reaction, including admitting you might be wrong.

wEwGBIr_RIw.summary: Cognitive biases are mental shortcuts that distort our judgment, such as relying on first information, following crowds, and ignoring facts, and knowing them helps us think more logically.

points.text: Anchoring bias means relying too heavily on the first information you get, so later numbers are judged against it, even when that first information is unreliable.
Availability heuristic: people overestimate the importance of information they hear often, like news stories, instead of judging danger by real facts and statistics.
The bandwagon effect is believing or doing something just because most others do, without thinking. Groupthink in meetings can silence a good idea.
Choice-supportive bias is defending a choice just because you made it, noticing its strengths and ignoring its flaws while stressing the flaws of alternatives.
Confirmation bias is favoring or interpreting information so it matches what you already believe, and it is especially dangerous in science.
Ostrich bias is choosing to ignore negative information or problems, hoping they will go away, like procrastinating on an assignment or smokers dismissing health risks.
Outcome bias is judging a decision as good or bad only by how it turned out, even if the result was luck, which leads to poor thinking over time.
Overconfidence is trusting your gut over facts after past successes. The gambler's fallacy shows past coin flips do not change the next flip's odds.
Survivorship bias is judging something only by the cases that survived, ignoring the many that did the same thing but failed, such as 'things millionaires do' articles.
Blind spot bias is believing you are less biased than other people, like a teacher who says gifts sway other teachers but never herself.

nYYkRaU0xh8.summary: Human minds have built-in thinking errors and mental shortcuts, such as anchoring, halo effect and confirmation bias, that quietly shape decisions, and noticing them makes you a more rational thinker.

points.text: Cognitive dissonance is holding two conflicting beliefs, like dismissing a job you failed to get as 'no good anyway'. It causes stress and anxiety, so you should choose one belief.
The spotlight effect is believing people watch and judge you far more than they really do; remembering this reduces anxiety.
The anchoring effect means a starting number, even a random one like a dice roll, pulls your later estimates toward it. Sellers exploit this with high opening prices.
To resist anchoring, remind yourself you are vulnerable to it and set your own mental anchor before a negotiation.
The halo effect is when one early trait or first impression outshines how you see the whole person or thing, so information order matters.
Gambler's fallacy is wrongly believing a balancing force makes a streak end. Independent events like coin flips have no memory of previous results.
The contrast effect makes something seem cheap or small when placed next to something bigger or pricier, so absolute judgments are hard.

Confirmation bias is interpreting new information to fit existing beliefs, seeking support and forgetting contrary evidence. Echo chambers strengthen it; use varied sources and 'think gray' to reduce it.
The Baader-Meinhof phenomenon is the illusion that something appears more often just because you have started noticing it.
The Zeigarnik effect makes unfinished tasks stick in memory. Writing down a plan to finish them is enough to quiet them.

ix2mdVIAbx8.summary: Memory problems are really problems of mental clarity, not storage, and precision in body and daily actions brings clarity and a stronger, more capable mind.

points.text: What we can achieve depends on our abilities, not on wishing; ability depends on how intelligently we act, which depends on how well the brain's wiring is connected.
Long mantra chanting was used to organize the brain's wiring, because the sounds, built with mathematics and poetry, affect what happens in the brain.
Such brain organization could give an almost impossible memory: the priest repeated an English conversation word for word without knowing the language, remembering only the sounds.
A simple first step to improve understanding and brain use is to learn to sit completely still, without moving.
Everything you see, hear, smell, taste and touch is recorded. The difficulty is only in retrieving it when needed.
Bad recall is like a faulty keyboard, not bad memory: pressing 2 and getting 5 is a keyboard fault. So the issue is clarity, not memory.
Let the mind copy the body's precision, and clarity will come naturally. A mind that practises this becomes a powerful tool you can direct as you wish.

mzexJPoXBCM.summary: Active recall, testing yourself by pulling information from memory instead of rereading or highlighting, is a hard but very time-efficient way to learn and remember material.

points.text: Read the material, step away, and try to remember specific details. Then go back and check what you missed.
Highlighting and underlining mostly involve motor commands, and they teach less than actively trying to remember the material.
Active recall means recreating the information from scratch, as if teaching a class, without looking at your notes.
Active recall is mentally taxing, which is why students avoid it, but it takes little time.
If you put up with the mental effort, you learn quickly and don't forget, and ideas come out almost fully formed on tests.
For math, active recall means doing proofs from a blank page. If you can't, you try again later.
Sort practice cards into a 'struggled' pile and a 'got it' pile, then keep working only the struggled pile. It shrinks fast.
Because it is efficient, you can master material in a few hours. Do it in the morning when you have energy, with no all-nighters.
Recall works by building a mental map. Mentally walk through it, and check your notes whenever you hit something you can't identify.

5wHyklLr_FA.summary: Focus works best when you narrow your sensory inputs, treat attention as a limited resource, and work in bursts with rest, letting hard thinking develop in the background.

points.text: Focus is like a ball bearing settling into a deepening trench as you go further into an activity; deep in it, you reach flow and forget yourself.
Many people who feel they can't concentrate may simply not be limiting their sensory inputs and context enough to drop into deep focus.
Changing your immediate environment, like moving to another cafe or seat, can break you out of a stuck point and re-anchor your attention.
A distraction-free workspace helps: the first 10 to 15 minutes are uncomfortable with every distracting thought, then they fade and you can work for hours.
Acetylcholine creates the attentional spotlight, anchoring thoughts and actions to a specific set of sensory inputs, while norepinephrine raises overall alertness.
A phone adds thousands of competing spheres of attention. Because acetylcholine is a limited resource spent during focus and replenished by sleep, focusing becomes very hard.
Attention can work like interval training: an athlete's focus span matches the length of their event, and they repeat short efforts with breaks.
Hard, effortful thinking takes its own time, so you can schedule downtime after planning and let ideas develop in the background.
Mental work needs rest and recovery like physical exercise, so trust your brain's shifting states instead of fighting them; being blocked may mean you don't yet know what comes next.

JKAjotzSrwA.summary: Because the brain can only process a little at once, attention selects what matters, and external things or inner thoughts compete for that limited capacity.

points.text: The brain has limited capacity and cannot process all incoming sensory information, so it would be wasteful to store everything.
Attention is the process that selects which information is important to you.
Bottom-up attention happens when a strong, important sensory stimulus, like a falling building, grabs your focus automatically.
Top-down attention is deliberate focus that filters out everything except what you are looking for, like a friend in a red dress.
Attention can also be captured by internal thoughts, not just outside objects; both compete for where the brain sends its resources.
Things compete for attention because of limited capacity, so you can focus processing on only a few elements at a time, maybe just one.
Being lost in your own thoughts has an energy cost, and effective people decide, then immerse in the task and turn down their inner noise, like a flow state.
Social media and other distractions may appeal because they spare people from thinking about their own thoughts.
Working memory is limited, so holding many options at once is hard; some people prefer narrowing choices to two or three.
The more items you hold in working memory, the worse the quality of memory for each one becomes.

TUoJc0NPajQ.summary: Memory is built by brain networks in three steps—encoding, consolidation, retrieval—and you can strengthen it through recall, sleep, diet, exercise, and mental challenge.

points.text: Each time you remember something, the hippocampus and other brain parts work together as a team, building the memory from scratch.
Encoding is the first step: your brain consciously registers the information so a memory can begin.
Forgetting a name right after meeting someone usually isn't a bad memory; the name was never encoded, often because you weren't paying attention.
Consolidation is the second step, acting like glue that holds the memory together.
Retrieval is the final step: a memory only counts as a memory once you recall it.
A regular sleep pattern and a balanced diet help memory, since the diet gives your brain the nutrients it needs.
Exercise helps memory by increasing the oxygen and nutrients flowing to your brain.
Learning new things and staying mentally active can physically enlarge your brain, keeping memory sharp.

BXZzhsYHvSw.summary: Mental models are hidden thinking shortcuts our minds use daily, and knowing them, like anchoring, loss aversion and status quo bias, helps us pause and decide better.

points.text: Mental models are hidden rules or shortcuts the brain uses every day to understand the world and decide quickly, though they are not always 100% correct.
Anchoring means the first number you see becomes a reference point, making later prices seem fair by comparison. Pause and ask whether the price is truly right.
Backward chaining means fixing the goal first, then planning step by step backward from it, so you don't get stuck midway or miss needed steps.
Commitment bias is the urge to stick to a promise to look consistent. It becomes harmful when we keep a promise even though it hurts us.
Margin of safety means arranging a bit more than you need where things are uncertain, to avoid last-minute trouble. Too much margin becomes waste, so balance it.
Survivorship bias is looking only at those who succeeded and forgetting the many who failed, so success seems easier than it is. Study failure rates too.
Reciprocity is the unwritten social rule that when someone does us a favour, we want to return it. It builds trust but can be used to pressure us.
Status quo bias is the tendency to keep things as they are and avoid change, even when better options exist. Ask whether the old way is best or just familiar.
These models are neither good nor bad; they are tools of how the mind works. Being aware of them lets us pause and choose better.

KetW0-gURJc.summary: Systems are defined by how their parts connect and what they aim for, so you improve them by understanding feedback, leverage, limits, boundaries, resilience and your own assumptions.

points.text: A system is more than a pile of parts. It is defined by how the parts connect and by its purpose.
Emergent behavior comes from the interactions between elements, not from any single element. This is why a team of average players can beat individual talent.
Systems run on two kinds of feedback loops: balancing loops keep things stable, like a thermostat, and reinforcing loops amplify change, like compounding interest.
Having a feedback loop is not enough. Feedback must be processed on time and effectively, because delays make a system unstable.
Leverage points are spots where a small change has a big impact. The strongest ones are paradigm shifts, system goals and information flows.
Growth has limits. Pushing endless growth on finite resources breaks the system, as when everyone overuses a shared resource until it runs out.
Shifting the burden means using quick fixes that hide the root cause. The system becomes dependent on them and grows weaker, so root causes must be addressed.
Every system sits inside a larger system. Optimizing only one part just moves the problem elsewhere, so you must widen the boundary you look at.
Resilience is a system's ability to recover from outside shocks. Chasing only efficiency can make a system fragile, so it also needs self-organization and coordinated hierarchy.
Mental models are simplified lenses that show only part of the truth. Test your assumptions, and measure more than one thing, such as productivity, engagement and creativity.

WyEnodich1w.summary: Mental models are thinking frameworks borrowed from physics and biology, and using many of them together helps you understand the world and decide better.

points.text: Reciprocity comes from Newton's third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. When you act on things, they act back on you.
Reciprocity is a mechanical system principle, not karma. Any energy you put into a system, good or bad, comes back to affect you, and no cosmic justice is needed.
Reciprocity can be exploited. A free gift creates a feeling of debt so you buy something back; knowing the principle helps you spot that pressure.
Entropy says disorder in a closed system always grows over time. Order in health, relationships or work only lasts if you keep spending energy on it.
Inertia, from Newton's first law, means things at rest or in motion keep doing so unless an outside force acts. Habits and comfortable routines behave the same way.
Beat inertia by lowering the activation energy: make the first step tiny, like putting on workout clothes or writing one sentence, to get momentum going.
Leverage means applying effort at the right point, the fulcrum, so a small push moves a big load. Hard work alone isn't enough, and leverage also magnifies losses.
Mental models work best as a connected lattice, not isolated tools. Reflecting on your decisions through journaling and applying one model right away builds real skill.

ocMH2l2ptpc.summary: Mental models are simplified representations of how the world works, and learning many of them gives you more lenses to see problems clearly and make better decisions.

points.text: A mental model is a simplified representation of how the world works, and using many models from different fields leaves you with fewer blind spots.
The map is not the territory: any representation, like a spreadsheet or report, is a reduction of reality, so get to know the real thing before deciding.
Your circle of competence is what you understand well. Decide confidently inside it, and consult an expert when a decision falls outside it.
Probabilistic thinking means estimating the likelihood of outcomes instead of treating them as yes or no, using prior information to judge how worried to be.
Inversion means starting from failure: work out what would cause it, then set goals and priorities to avoid those causes.
Occam's Razor says the simpler explanation is more likely true, because it has fewer moving parts that all need to be proven.
Hanlon's Razor says not to assume malice when incompetence or ignorance explains a behavior, such as a friend not replying because they are busy.
Reciprocity means people tend to return how you treat them, so kindness brings kindness and poor treatment brings poor treatment back.
Activation energy is the push needed to start something. Catalysts like coffee or inspiration lower it, so find what makes starting hard and reduce it.

S5SBcAuqCSg.summary: Chess offers five mental models—control the center, know a piece's true value, position before submission, own the initiative, and the hardest move—that help you make better strategic decisions in business and life.

points.text: A mental model is a ready-made framework you use for decisions: plug in the variables and get an answer, which builds good judgment in a repeatable way.
Control the center: pieces in the middle influence more squares than pieces in corners. Ask where your board's center is and put your resources there.
With limited resources, focus on the one or two key squares. For weight loss, nutrition beats exercise. For a new business, fix product first, then customers.
A piece's true value depends on its position and board dynamics, not just its point count. Likewise, people's value depends on their abilities and where you place them.
For a problem, ask "who do I know that could help?" rather than only "how do I solve this?" The right person can make it much easier.
Position before submission: skilled players secure a dominant position first, and the winning move then appears. Beginners chase the one-shot kill and weaken their position.
There is no hack. Hunting for one distracts you from the slow work of controlling your position, which leads to success. Environment design is one way to do it.
The initiative means dictating the action: you act while your opponent reacts. The player with the initiative usually wins, even with weaker forces.

T5-re2X-YSY.summary: Solve hard problems by inverting them: ask how you'd fail or cause harm, then avoid it, while sticking to basics and not over-analyzing.

points.text: Inversion means asking the opposite question: instead of how to succeed, ask what would cause failure or harm, then work to avoid exactly that.
Inverting shrinks a big problem to a few key hazards. As a forecaster, Munger found only two ways to kill a pilot: icing or running out of fuel.
Inversion works like algebra: many practical problems become easy when flipped and stay hard when approached head-on.
Even big goals can be inverted: rather than asking how to help India, ask what would hurt it most, which exposes vulnerabilities to avoid.
Real-world problems must be thought through in all their real dimensions. The appraiser used two dimensions and missed the damage towers do by freezing land grade.
Experts fail when they ignore fundamentals. Constantly returning to basics catches errors that trained specialists miss, and it raised the easement value from $125,000 to $600,000.
If a problem resists, keep turning it over from different angles and attack it hard, then return to it. A toolbox of mental tricks lets ordinary minds get exceptional results.
Certainty doesn't need to be perfect: being about 96% sure is often all you're entitled to, so decide once the key facts are clear.
Excessive due diligence often signals weak thinking and insecurity. Focus on the few obvious facts, such as a great asset and a good deal, rather than combing through every detail.

_XkNf5NgU1Y.summary: Systems thinking means looking at the connections and feedback loops between parts, not straight cause-and-effect, so you can spot common traps and find leverage points for big change.

points.text: Linear thinking assumes one cause leads to one effect, but it often fails because it ignores the hidden web of connections that actually runs a situation.
Linear fixes can backfire. Cutting calories makes you hungrier, slows your metabolism and adds stress, so your own solution creates a backlash from the system.
The key shift is to look at the connections between things, not just the individual parts, because a system's real behavior lives in those relationships.
A system is more than the sum of its parts. A football team is its plays, communication, strategy and trust, not just eleven players and a ball.
A system's behavior comes from its underlying structure, not one-off events, just as a slinky bounces because of how it is coiled, not because of your hand.
A reinforcing loop is a snowball effect: more leads to even more, causing exponential growth that can quickly get out of control, like interest on money in a bank.
A balancing loop is goal-seeking and stabilizing. It shrinks the gap to a target, like a hot coffee cooling to room temperature or your body holding its temperature.
Combined loops create classic traps: escalation (an arms race of reactions), tragedy of the commons (individual gain, shared cost), and shifting the burden (quick fixes that worsen the real problem).
A leverage point is a spot where a small, well-placed push changes the whole system, like a trim tab steering a huge ship's rudder.
Making feedback visible can be a leverage point. Homes with the electric meter in the hallway used about 30% less electricity because people saw their usage in real time.

cosjtcWyWlI.summary: Compounding means a steady growth rate applied to an ever-larger base, so money grows slowly at first then sharply, and real markets reach the same end point through bumpy ups and downs.

points.text: Compounding means growing at a fixed rate, but each year's growth is calculated on a new, bigger base that includes earlier gains.
With 10% growth, the rate stays the same every year, but the rupees earned rise each year (10, 11, 12.1...) because the base keeps growing.
Compounding makes an exponential curve, which looks almost flat for a long time and then takes off very fast.
The growth rate doesn't depend on the size of your money. The same stock growing 10% gives 10% on ₹100 or on ₹1 crore.
Real markets don't grow in a straight line. Nifty's monthly and yearly returns from 2000 to 2020 swung up and down, with some negative years.
CAGR is the single steady yearly rate that turns your starting amount into the final amount: (final ÷ starting) to the power 1/years, minus 1.
Nifty's bumpy path ended at the same point as a smooth 11.78% yearly curve, so both views reach the same final amount.
Don't expect smooth yearly growth. Compounding works only if you handle uncertainty and stay invested through the ups and downs.

HZGCoVF3YvM.summary: Bayes' theorem shows that new evidence should update your prior belief by the proportion of cases with the evidence where the hypothesis is also true, which is easy to see with samples or areas.

points.text: Rationality is not about knowing facts but about recognizing which facts are relevant, such as the ratio of farmers to librarians when judging who Steve is.
New evidence does not fully determine your beliefs on its own. It should update the beliefs you already held.
The prior is the probability of the hypothesis before seeing evidence. The likelihood is the probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is true.
Bayes' theorem: P(H|E) equals P(H) times P(E|H), divided by the total probability of the evidence. The denominator adds the hypothesis-true and hypothesis-false cases. The result is the posterior.
Instead of memorizing the formula, draw a 1x1 square of all possibilities. Events are areas, and evidence restricts the square to a lopsided region.
Evidence that is equally likely under both sides leaves your belief unchanged. The more different the likelihoods are, the more your belief shifts.
Thinking in specific counts, like 40 out of 100, engages intuition better than percentages. This made the Linda error disappear.
Probability math is really the math of proportions. Bayes' theorem says to look at cases where the evidence is true and find what share also has the hypothesis true.
Debates about Steve's context change the prior, while debates about personality stereotypes change the likelihoods. Both can be pictured in the diagram.

9wCnvr7Xw4E.summary: Bayes' theorem lets you get one conditional probability from its reverse, even without the joint probability, which is useful when you only have partial or guessed data.

points.text: Dividing counts by the total population turns them into probabilities. This gives the same answer (0.71) but now shows the joint probability divided by the probability of the known fact.
Conditional probability is the chance an event happens, scaled by knowledge we already have about it, such as dividing 'not love candy and love soda' by 'love soda'.
Changing what we already know changes the result. The event stays the same and the numerator stays the same, but the scaling differs, so we get 0.63 instead of 0.71.
Multiplying each conditional probability equation by its denominator shows that both equal the same joint probability, the chance of meeting someone who does not love candy and loves soda.
Because both expressions equal the same joint probability, they equal each other. Dividing by the right term isolates each conditional probability without needing the joint probability.
Bayes' theorem says a conditional probability given one piece of knowledge can be found from the reverse conditional probability, using the two single-event probabilities.
With a full data table, Bayes' theorem is no big deal. It matters when data is missing and you only know some probabilities, so you plug those into the formula.
Bayes' theorem still works with guessed values, though the answer differs from the exact one (0.75 versus 0.71). Guessing is often the only option for large populations.
Bayes' theorem is the basis of Bayesian statistics, which pairs the equation with a broader philosophy of how statistics should be calculated, including what it means to make a guess.
Standard notation drops the known fact from the event, so two conditional probabilities look like different events. Both refer to the same area, and only the given knowledge differs.

sxYrzzy3cq8.summary: Statistics can mislead because a hidden factor can reverse a trend when data is grouped differently, a pattern called Simpson's paradox, so we must study the real situation behind the numbers.

points.text: Statistics are persuasive, so people and countries base big decisions on them, but a set of data can hide something that turns the results upside down.
Overall numbers can point to one choice: Hospital A saved 900 of 1000 patients and Hospital B saved 800, so A looks better.
Patients do not all arrive equally healthy, so splitting data into good-health and poor-health groups can change the picture completely.
After splitting the groups, Hospital B has better survival rates for both poor-health and good-health patients, even though Hospital A looked better overall.
Simpson's paradox is when the same data shows opposite trends depending on how it is grouped.
It often happens when combined data hides a lurking variable, a hidden extra factor that strongly influences results, like the mix of patient health in the hospitals.
Simpson's paradox happens in real life: a UK study made smokers look like they survived more, until age groups showed nonsmokers were much older on average.
In Florida death penalty cases, overall rates hid a racial disparity; splitting by victim's race showed black defendants were more likely to be sentenced to death either way.
There is no single fix, since overall numbers are sometimes more accurate than data split into arbitrary categories.
To avoid being fooled, study the real situation the statistics describe and ask whether lurking variables are present; otherwise others can manipulate you with data.

bVG2OQp6jEQ.summary: True statistics can still mislead through how numbers are framed, mixed up, or graphed, so you must ask what the numbers really mean.

points.text: Statistics can be powerful: shopping patterns like more lotion and vitamin purchases let Target predict which customers were pregnant and their due dates.
A claim can be technically true yet misleading. '80% of dentists recommend Colgate' let dentists pick several brands, so other brands could score as high or higher.
A percentage increase can exaggerate a tiny change. Going from 1 in 7,000 to 2 in 7,000 is a '100% increase' but only about 0.014% more.
Correlation means two things move together; it does not prove one causes the other. People often wrongly assume A causes B just because they are linked.
Two correlated things may both be caused by a third factor. Hot weather drives both ice cream sales and heat strokes, though neither causes the other.

Simpson's paradox: overall totals can tell the opposite story from grouped data. Berkeley's overall rates looked biased against women, but by department it flipped, because women applied to harder programs.
Bar graphs whose baseline is not zero make small differences look huge. A rise under 15% can look like several hundred percent.

OTGFdxd1zag.summary: Speaking English becomes easy to start by learning many short phrases you can use in conversation without grammar, practised by repeating them aloud with the teacher.

points.text: Short phrases are small ready-made English chunks, like 'I'm sorry' or 'Thank you', that you can use in conversation without building a full sentence.
Speaking a full English sentence at the start is hard, so split it: say the short phrase in English and the rest in Hindi.
'Let me know' is a useful short phrase; mixing it into a Hindi sentence makes a good impression and starts your English speaking.
You already use phrases like 'I don't know' without trouble because you say them in flow without thinking much, so more phrases means an easier start.
Day one gives 200 short phrases, plus a free PDF in the teacher's app, so you can begin speaking from today.
Echo practice: the teacher says each sentence twice, and you speak along with her the second time.
To really learn, stay until the end and practise every phrase aloud, not just watch.
Many everyday phrases are commands or requests, like 'Don't overthink', 'Let it go', 'Hold on', 'Hurry up' and 'Take care'.
Common questions can also be short phrases, such as 'What's going on?', 'Is it possible?', 'Do you know?' and 'Are you ready?'.

hM1hah6ELO8.summary: Speak English in 21 days by practising seven habits: listen a lot, say words aloud, read loudly, describe pictures, train your mouth, use a mirror, and build confidence.

points.text: Studying grammar and dictionaries first is a poor way to learn speaking. Start with listening instead.
Learn English the way you learned your first language: by listening. Watch English movies, series, commentary and news so your brain absorbs the language.
Spend 10 minutes daily naming everything you see in your room in English, using single words. Start small instead of memorising long paragraphs.
Read an English book aloud, slowly but loudly. Using more senses helps the brain learn English faster, and getting stuck on words is fine.
Picture method: look at an image and describe what you see in English sentences. Daily practice makes it easier to say things in English.
Before sleeping, spend 10 minutes recalling your day in English, even if broken. This helps you speak the English thoughts you already have in your mind.
Pen-pencil trick: hold a pen between your teeth and say the vowels daily. It trains your tongue to speak English clearly.
Mirror method: speak English in front of a mirror to check your hand movements and facial expressions. Speaking English correctly involves body language, not just words.
Record a one-minute English video every day for 21 days. Comparing day 1 with day 21 shows your progress and builds fluency.
Confidence matters more than perfect grammar. Speaking with a smile, even in broken English, makes people believe you know English, so don't fear being judged.

Sj7n5znCytc.summary: The video teaches 50 useful English words with their Hindi meanings to help learners speak English in daily life.

points.text: Sympathy means feeling for someone else's trouble; the Hindi meaning is हमदर्दी.
Innocent means मासूम, someone who is pure and has done no wrong. Recognize means to identify someone or something (पहचानना).
Possible means something can happen (संभव). Impossible is its opposite, meaning it cannot happen (असंभव).
War means युद्ध, and attack means to strike someone (हमला करना).
A stranger is a person you do not know, called अजनबी in Hindi.
Worship means पूजा, and a temple is the place for it (मंदिर).
Comparison means तुलना, judging two things side by side. Concern means चिंता, a feeling of worry.

RKK7wGAYP6k.summary: The language you speak shapes how you think, affecting your sense of space, time, number, color, gender and blame, as recent scientific research now shows.

points.text: Language lets humans move complex thoughts between minds, even brand-new ideas, by turning sounds and air vibrations into thoughts in the listener's brain.
The big question is whether the language we speak shapes how we think. People argued about it for thousands of years without data, but labs now test it scientifically.
Kuuk Thaayorre speakers use compass directions instead of left and right, so they constantly track direction and stay oriented far better than we thought humans could.
Kuuk Thaayorre speakers lay out time according to compass direction, east to west, not relative to their body. Time is locked onto the landscape.
Counting is a linguistic trick. People whose languages lack exact number words struggle to track exact quantities, and number words open up mathematics.
Words for colors change perception. Russian has separate words for light and dark blue, so Russian speakers tell those shades apart faster, and their brains register the change.
Grammatical gender colors how people see objects. German speakers describe a bridge (feminine in German) as beautiful or elegant, while Spanish speakers (masculine) say strong or long.
How a language describes events affects what speakers remember. English speakers recall who caused an accident, while Spanish speakers more often recall that it was an accident.
Wording guides blame and punishment. People blame and punish more when told "He broke it" than "It broke," even when they watch the same event.
Language effects can be big, deep, early, broad, and personal. Knowing this lets you ask why you think as you do and how you could think differently.

0TFNVP6r_-o.summary: The languages we speak shape how we think, from how we handle space, time, color and gender to how we remember events and assign blame.

points.text: Thousands of languages differ in sounds, words and structure, which raises the question of whether speakers of different languages think differently. Scientific evidence has only recently begun to answer it.
Some languages, like Kuuk Thaayorre, use cardinal directions (north, south, east, west) instead of left and right. Speakers must always know their heading, so they stay oriented remarkably well.
Human orientation skill is not limited by biology. It comes from linguistic and cultural practice, showing our brains can do more than we assume because we are used to less.

Languages divide colors differently. Russian has separate words for light blue and dark blue, so Russian speakers distinguish colors across that boundary faster, and their brains register a category change.
Wording changes blame and punishment even when people see the event themselves. Hearing "he broke the vase" makes people more likely to blame someone and demand more damages.

Linguistic diversity shows the ingenuity of the human mind, yet half of today's languages may vanish within a hundred years. Losing them narrows science, which mostly studies English-speaking American undergraduates.

FWTNMzK9vG4.summary: Procrastination is not laziness or poor time management but the body's stress response to a task it sees as threatening, so reducing negative emotions, not self-punishment, breaks the cycle.

points.text: Procrastination is avoiding a task you said you would do, for no good reason, even though you expect negative consequences. Sensible delaying of less important tasks is not procrastination.
Procrastination comes from the body trying to protect us by avoiding a task it sees as threatening.
The amygdala releases hormones like adrenaline, starting a fear response that can overpower the prefrontal cortex, which normally helps with long-term thinking and emotional control.
We mostly put off tasks that trigger negative feelings like dread, incompetence, and insecurity, and a task seems harder while we are avoiding it.
People who struggle to regulate emotions or have low self-esteem are more likely to procrastinate, no matter how good their time management is.
Procrastinators are not simply lazy. Laziness means low energy and apathy, while many procrastinators care too much and fear their work won't meet their high standards.
Procrastination brings long-term harm like anxiety, shame, and stress, yet it briefly lowers stress, which reinforces it as a coping habit.
Being harsh on yourself adds bad emotions to a task and makes the threat feel bigger, so the fix is reducing negative emotions rather than strict discipline.
Helpful strategies include splitting a task into smaller parts, journaling about what stresses you, and removing nearby distractions.
Self-compassion helps: forgive yourself and make a plan to do better next time.

wr6fQ4KpbRM.summary: Habits are automatic cue-behavior-reward loops built by the brain, so breaking them works best by changing cues and environments or replacing the behavior, not by willpower alone.

points.text: A habit is a behavior done regularly and triggered subconsciously by a cue in the environment, such as a place, time of day, or emotional state.
Habits form because the brain learns a behavior is beneficial, like nail-biting easing anxiety after a stressful email.
Rewards release dopamine, which changes how neurons wire, linking the reward to the behavior and pushing you to repeat it.
Over time the behavior gets tied to cues like your environment, so just sitting at your desk can trigger the habit without any stress or reward.
Habit loops run faster than decision-making, so you may act before noticing. This helps with good habits, which are stored memories that save time and mental energy.
Good intentions alone often fail to create lasting change, but understanding how habits work lets you make better plans to change them.
Identify the places or times that cue a habit, then change your routine or add obstacles that make the habit harder there.
Big life changes, like moving or switching schools or jobs, remove old cues, making them good moments to break or build habits.
Habit reversal training replaces a habit with a less harmful one, after you analyze your cues so you can step in at the right times.

7KBxvfz4mQk.summary: Procrastination is a changeable choice, not a character flaw; beat it short-term with timers, small steps and accountability, and long-term with realistic goals and a supportive environment.

points.text: Procrastination is not your fault or a sign you are a bad person. It is a choice you can change, so guilt over it does not help.
The Pomodoro technique means working 25 minutes, then taking a 5-minute break. Looking forward to the break helps you stay focused during the work.
The two-minute rule: if a task can be done in about two minutes (or five, if you set your own limit), do it right now instead of delaying it.
Big goals feel like huge mountains. Like a map, break the goal into small steps and picture each one, and it stops feeling overwhelming.
Time blocking means reserving a slot in your day and promising to finish a specific task before that slot ends.
An accountability partner is someone who checks whether you finished. Not wanting to let down their trust makes you more likely to do the work.
For the long term, set goals you can actually achieve, not ones imposed by society. Achievable goals, like a diet with room for sweets, are easier to follow.
Your environment shapes your habits: the content you consume and the people around you. Choose friends and colleagues who encourage you and are positive.
Exercise and good nutrition help fight procrastination because body and mind are connected. Feeling fit makes you naturally get up and act.

Ybk63zjfSL8.summary: A morning routine that gives you protected time for your mind, body, and learning sets you up for the day, and it works at any start time as long as you keep one.

points.text: Your morning routine really begins the night before, so ending the evening with reading and going to sleep on time sets up an early wake-up.
Start the day with 15 quiet minutes and a glass of water, with no phone, books, music or people, instead of rushing straight into work.
Meditate for about half an hour in one calm spot, using an app with nature sounds and bells every ten minutes to mark time.
Read books on a Kindle and highlight as you go. Afterwards, export the highlights, reread them, and turn the useful ones into an action plan.
Don't try to memorise a book. Apply what fits your life and move on from what doesn't.
Reading 30 to 45 minutes daily adds up to hours each week. Pick books you enjoy, with no pressure or race.
Exercise daily, with tennis followed by about 45 minutes of gym work. Lifting heavier weights builds more muscle, while adding reps builds muscle endurance.
Skim two newspapers for the important headlines instead of watching TV news, and skip sports and current-affairs sections that waste time.
Eat only two meals inside a six-hour window, with an 18-hour fast, in a controlled way, which he says helps fat loss and muscle gain.
A morning routine gives you hours for yourself before work, making you hard to shake. Start at any time, but have a routine.

dqONk48l5vY.summary: Sleep is essential because it lets the brain clear out daily waste products, and going without it harms the mind and body, sometimes fatally.

points.text: Going without sleep damages thinking and mood: focus, touch, coordination, memory, and even a sense of reality can break down, as in Randy Gardner's 11-day experiment.
Adults need about seven to eight hours of sleep a night, and adolescents need about ten.
Tiredness signals from the body and darkness signals from the environment raise sleep-inducing chemicals like adenosine and melatonin, which bring on sleep.
In non-REM sleep, breathing and heart rate slow, muscles relax, DNA is repaired, and the body restores itself for the next day.
Lack of sleep harms the body, affecting learning, memory, mood, and reaction time, and it is linked to inflammation, high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, and stroke.
Chronically sleeping under six hours a night raises stroke risk four and a half times compared with getting seven to eight hours.
Fatal Familial Insomnia is a rare inherited mutation that prevents sleep and leads to dementia and death within months or years.
While awake, cells use energy and produce byproducts like adenosine. Its buildup creates sleep pressure, and caffeine works by blocking adenosine's receptors.
Scientists think sleep deprivation is harmful because waste products build up in the brain and, if not cleared, overload it.
The glymphatic system is the brain's cleanup mechanism, much more active during sleep, using cerebrospinal fluid to flush toxic byproducts from between cells.

hmFQqjMF_f0.summary: Playing a sport you enjoy, especially on a team, gives physical and mental exercise benefits plus extra psychological gains like community, confidence, resilience and a growth mindset.

points.text: Exercise strengthens bones, clears bad cholesterol from arteries, and lowers the risk of stroke, high blood pressure, and diabetes, especially when started young.
Working out releases brain chemicals like endorphins, natural hormones controlling pain and pleasure, which can cause a feeling of euphoria called a runner's high.
Endorphins and regular physical activity sharpen focus and improve mood and memory.
Playing a sport and team you like brings benefits beyond what exercise alone gives, and the biggest ones are psychological, in both short and long term.
Being on a team teaches you to trust, depend on, help, and accept help from others while working toward a shared goal.
Commitment to a fun team makes it easier to build a regular exercise habit, and school sport lowers depression risk for up to four years.
Repeated practice, especially with a good coach, builds a growth mindset: believing you can improve through practice even if you can't do something today.
Learning from failure builds resilience and self-awareness, helping you handle academic, social, and physical challenges, so even a losing team offers real benefit.
Not every sport suits everyone, so it's okay to search until you find one that fits your needs and strengths.

b53BXGfd58Y.summary: Sleep is an active process that restores the brain and body, and sleeping under seven hours quietly hurts focus, memory, and safety, so it is not wasted time.

points.text: Sleep is not a passive switch-off. It is an active process where the brain and body work to restore themselves.
During sleep, what you learned moves into long-term memory, immunity gets a boost, and your brain and body relax and restore, like a servicing.
Research says sleeping more than seven hours is needed for understanding, concentration, memory, and good physical and mental health.
Short sleep does not give you extra time. The waking hours you gain are poorly used because focus and concentration suffer.
Sitting with a book is not enough; information must actually enter the brain. A tired brain cannot absorb it, so one focused hour beats two empty hours.
Ten days in a row of seven hours or less makes your brain perform like that of someone who has not slept for 24 hours.
Sleep-deprived people often cannot tell they are impaired. They may wrongly accept low sharpness, memory, or energy as just how they are.
Broken or poor sleep is dangerous. Next-day drowsiness raises accident risk when driving, reportedly even more than drunk driving.

UsnJvYq-2BM.summary: Anxiety and stress are normal responses, but when they grow too strong they need treatment, and habits like diet, less caffeine and time with loved ones can help.

points.text: Stress is a normal, simple response of the body and mind.
Anxiety is the fear you feel about something unknown.
Some anxiety is completely normal. Every person feels it at some point.
When anxiety grows far too strong, it becomes a real problem and needs treatment.
Changing your diet, for example by adding ashwagandha, can leave you feeling a bit more relaxed and calm.
Reduce caffeine intake, because drinking a lot of coffee affects anxiety.
Cigarettes and tobacco may seem to relieve stress, but they only make you feel better for a short time, so avoid them.
Spending time with the people close to you can reduce stress a great deal.
A panic attack is a sudden burst of panic lasting around 15 minutes.
A frightening event like an earthquake can leave lasting fear, so the person is afraid to go back to the place where it happened.

wf91rEGw88Q.summary: Compound interest earns interest on both the original money and past interest, so it grows faster than simple interest, especially over long periods.

points.text: Compound interest is interest earned on your original investment plus all the interest that has built up over time, so it is interest on interest.
Simple interest is interest earned only on the original principal, never on interest already earned.
With simple interest, the interest is the same every year. $10,000 at 5% earns $500 a year, or $1,500 over three years.
With compounding, year one's interest matches simple interest ($500), because only the original principal has earned anything so far.
In year two, interest is calculated on the original amount plus year one's interest. 5% of $10,500 is $525.
In year three, interest is calculated on the principal plus all earlier interest: 5% of $11,025 gives $551.25.
Over three years, compounding earns $1,576.25 versus $1,500 for simple interest, a gain of $76.25 from the same deposit and rate.
Compounding gets more powerful over longer periods because the interest earned keeps getting larger and larger.

_7J1JVCxWJM.summary: Instead of strict budgets, make small changes to everyday spending on eating out, delivery, and shopping so you spend less and get more happiness from your money.

points.text: Most budgets fail because people stop tracking, and most of a budget is fixed costs like rent, phone, and car payments that can't change without major life decisions.
The real struggle is small, frequent purchases like eating out, delivery services, and shopping, so each one should be tackled separately.
A frequency budget limits how many times you eat out instead of how much you spend, which is easier to track and easier to say no to.
You can meet your social craving without eating out, using cheaper activities like picnics with friends or workout classes.
Delivery apps cost more because of extra charges and fees, and the same item can even cost more on the app than in the restaurant.
Spending on others, on experiences, and on things that save you time makes you happier than other kinds of spending.
Spending even a small amount, like 5 dollars, on someone else can make you happier than spending it on yourself, so buy a gift or donate.
Paying for help like lawn mowing or house cleaning is worthwhile when you're overwhelmed, because the time saved is worth the price.
Small changes to discretionary spending let you spend less while getting more satisfaction, meaning fewer guilty pleasures and less regret.

MVd0SOappiQ.summary: Pay your future self first by investing before spending, and sort spending into needs, wants and investments so wants like status purchases don't crowd out saving.

points.text: To see where money goes, split spending into needs, wants and investments, and check how much each takes.
Whether something is a need or a want depends on your situation. The same car became a need once the commute had no practical alternative.
A healthy split settled at about 50% needs, 12% wants and around 40% investments, so needs shrank and investing grew as income rose.
Mistake one: buying things you don't need, like a bike, to show off. Young people in their 20s often play this status game.
Mistake two: leaving all savings idle in a bank account. Some of it could have been invested instead of fearing risk.
The poor person's habit is to spend first and save only what is left over, so saving often ends up tiny.
The rich person's habit is to pay yourself first: invest right after salary arrives, then live on what remains.
Needs like rent, loan EMIs and family support can't be cut, so make room to invest by trimming wants. You can still live well.

b6NP2fIThPQ.summary: Compounding means small, regular improvements or returns add up over many years into something big, in skills and in money, but only if you give it time.

points.text: Finding something you care about and practising it is the start; Joshi Uncle found his passion in pickle-making after trying many other things.
Compounding is small improvements made regularly that keep adding up over many years until they become big.
Tiny improvements made every day, even if each looks small, stack up until you become the best at your craft.
Compounding works in every part of life, such as school, hobbies and jobs, when you keep improving a little each day.
Compounding also works with money: you invest what you have, it earns small regular returns, and over years those returns add up and grow large.
Investing means putting your money into something, like buying cashew peda to resell, hoping to earn more money from it.
Repeating the investing again and again, reusing earlier profits, is compounding your money, as the children's plan tried to do.
To grow rich, combine both: improve daily at your passion until you master it, earn money from it, then invest that money so it compounds.
Compounding never happens overnight; you must give it a lot of time.

LgUCyWhJf6s.summary: Emotional intelligence is a learned skill for understanding our own and others' feelings wisely, and teaching it through education and culture is vital for humanity's future.

points.text: Emotional intelligence is the ability to face the problems in our relationships with ourselves and others using patience, insight and imagination.
Every kind of intelligence is an ability to handle a certain set of challenges. Clever, rich or powerful people who are unhappy or intolerant lack emotional intelligence.
With others, emotional intelligence means noticing their moods and reading what lies beneath the surface, such as an angry outburst that is really a hidden plea for help.
With ourselves, emotional intelligence means doubting our first impulses, since hatred may hide love, anger may cover sadness, and we often misjudge what we truly want.
Emotionally intelligent people meet failure with resilience and humor, and see well-handled pessimism as useful for a good life.
Emotional intelligence is not inborn. It is learned through education about our emotions, where they come from in childhood, and how to handle our fears and wishes.
Humans have grown technically skilled but not wiser, so we are like evolved monkeys with nuclear weapons. Civilization's fate depends on mastering emotional education.
Emotional education goes beyond classrooms and does not stop at 21. Culture, from high art to popular media, is the main way to pass it on.
Culture can carry emotional lessons in tragedies, TV series, pop songs, novels, buildings or YouTube films, pointing us toward greater emotional intelligence.

coiCkmcKjX8.summary: Anger comes from hidden optimism, hopes that reality keeps defeating, so becoming more pessimistic about how life goes is the way to grow calmer.

points.text: Angry people seem gloomy, but underneath they are deeply optimistic, and this optimism costs them.
Anger shows up when everyday things go wrong, like being interrupted, losing keys, or facing a delayed flight. Each time, the person is shouting because they hoped for better.
Angry people keep faith in an ideal world, where partners understand them, items never go missing, and schedules hold, even though experience keeps proving otherwise.
Every time these hopes are dashed, the angry person screams, and years of disappointment do not weaken the hopes.
We usually cannot remove life's frustrations, but we can change what they mean to us by accepting reality as the sadder thing it truly is.
Accepting dark truths helps: partners rarely understand each other well, we keep losing things that matter, and travel is full of delays.
More broadly, life apart from a few sunny patches is a run of disappointments, misunderstandings, sorrows, and griefs, ending in catastrophe.
Most of us are a bit like Fred, but our agitation is temporary. It results from our expectations suddenly being defeated.
To become reliably calmer, we should be much less optimistic about how life might go. Pessimism is the cure for anger.

J8fhvToxIfI.summary: Anger is managed by pausing before reacting, planning your words in advance, and trying to see the other person's point of view.

points.text: Anger management in one sentence: delay your response instead of reacting instantly.
The mind has two parts: the emotional brain runs on feelings, while the rational brain thinks things through.
The emotional brain reacts first and instantly, without thinking further, so its responses are often wrong or messy.
The rational brain answers minutes later but gives a more mature reply. Waiting 15-20 minutes makes your reaction more measured.
Answering anger with anger turns a conflict into a contest of hurting each other, and both people lose. If one person holds back, the problem can stop growing.
Anticipate the problem: predict how a tense situation may go and think ahead before entering it, so you can choose your words wisely.
Opening with an open question instead of an accusation invites a helpful answer, while blaming makes the other person defend themselves.
People get angry at how something is said, not at what is said. Polite, respectful wording gets a different response.
Empathize: in conflict we see only our own view. Imagining yourself in the other person's place helps you understand why they acted that way.
Getting angry solves nothing, since anger breeds more anger. Handling things better protects your own mental peace.

27UjxV4yBTc.summary: Anger comes from not knowing how your own mind works, so you can't decide what happens inside you, even though you can't control what people do to you.

points.text: How you deal with anger depends on who it is aimed at. You act differently with your mother, a friend or a professor.
Other people and things around us will often do what we dislike. That is normal.
You can't make sure only what you want happens around you, but you can decide that only what you want happens inside you.
Nobody gave you a user manual for yourself, so you never learned how your own system works.
Angry parents or grandparents should not become the inspiration or model for how you live.
Anger, fear, stress and anxiety appear when the mind isn't given proper instructions, because you don't know how to run it.
Your mind is like a supercomputer given to you without your knowing where the keyboard is, so you just fumble with it.
Trying random things on yourself sometimes works and sometimes doesn't. When it works, that is only coincidence, not real understanding.

foLf5Bi9qXs.summary: Caffeine keeps us awake by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain, stopping the molecule that makes neurons slow down, and the brain adapts to regular use.

points.text: Caffeine is a stimulant for the central nervous system; it keeps us awake by blocking adenosine, one of the body's key sleep-inducing molecules.
Adenosine is released when the body breaks down ATP for energy. It docks to receptors on brain neurons, making them fire sluggishly, so you feel sleepy.
Caffeine is an adenosine receptor antagonist: it is similar enough to adenosine to wedge into the receptors, but not similar enough to activate them.
Adenosine inhibits neurons, and caffeine blocks that inhibitor, so the net result is stimulation.
Some adenosine receptors are paired with dopamine receptors. Adenosine blocks dopamine from fitting in; when caffeine takes adenosine's place, dopamine can act and boost pleasure.
Caffeine can help the body burn fat and may lower risks of some diseases, so some sports bodies have limited athletes' caffeine levels.
Caffeine also has downsides: it can raise heart rate and blood pressure, and contribute to insomnia, anxiety, and other unpleasant effects.
With regular caffeine use, the brain makes extra adenosine receptors, so you need more caffeine to feel as alert.
Quitting caffeine suddenly causes withdrawal, because many receptors and no caffeine let adenosine work overtime. After a few days the extra receptors disappear and the body readjusts.

UMAELCrJxt0.summary: Inflation is the general rise of prices, caused by rising costs, rising demand, or printed money, and it is harmful mainly because prices and incomes don't rise evenly.

points.text: Prices and incomes keep rising over time, so money buys less than it once did; a cinema ticket cost 30p in 1970 and £13 today.
Governments track inflation closely and try to keep it low, because societies have learned to measure and manage it.
Cost-push inflation happens when businesses' costs rise, such as raw materials, wages or land rents, and they pass those costs on to customers through higher prices.
Demand inflation happens when more people want something than can be supplied. Getting richer, tax cuts, lower interest rates and easier credit can all push demand up.
Printing money causes inflation: more money chases the same goods, so each note is worth less and prices go up rather than people buying more.
Inflation does harm because not everything rises at the same rate. If all prices and incomes rose equally and predictably, it would be weird but harmless.
Inflation is bad for savings, since money set aside loses its worth. Keeping inflation low rewards prudence and lets people plan for the future.
Low inflation is hard to achieve because many factors can derail it, so inflation is like the weather or our moods: unstable, something we must endure while limiting extremes.

DNXnX-ybBjI.summary: Pain after a lost relationship is a mental and emotional problem, so shape your own inner state consciously and live wholeheartedly for others while staying ready to move on gracefully.

points.text: The body's basic life process needs food, air and water, but the life-force itself seems complete and does not need another person to support it.
The strong need for another person comes from the nature of your thoughts and emotions, and at certain life stages perhaps your body too.
Physical needs can be forgotten when your mind is absorbed. Reading a thriller for two hours, you don't think of food, so going beyond bodily needs is easy.
The problem of loss is essentially psychological: it is mental and emotional, not a physical matter.
Your mental structure should be built by you, consciously. Built with awareness, it can become a joyful possibility instead of a sad one.
Nobody wants suffering for themselves, so if you suffer, you have not shaped your mind with awareness the way you want it.
Live today as if ready to die for this person, but if they are gone tomorrow, move on with grace.
Treating relationships as cold logic, asking why an independent being needs anyone, makes life ugly and removes its purity.
People fall into two traps: becoming ruthless, or becoming so weak and withdrawn that they cannot enjoy their relationships.
Your good relationships should come from who you are, not from how others are. Either let the world live in your shade, or keep craving someone else's.

EPdNs93yyMw.summary: Curiosity, backed by the courage to act on it, works like a superpower that opens up new people, opportunities, and understanding.

points.text: Curiosity can be your greatest attribute, a kind of superpower, but only if you have the courage to actually use it.
Curiosity does not depend on past results. Even with a report card of all F's, someone can be told they will be special and go far.
