Curiosity becomes powerful when you apply it in a bigger way, not just feel it, such as reaching out to someone you admire.
Being persistent helps you reach people. When a meeting was hard to get, showing up in person and waiting for the professor worked.
A small, low-pressure request is easier to accept. Asking for only ten minutes and a coffee, with no big ask, got a yes.
A short meeting can grow into a deep conversation, and one such talk can teach more than a year in a classroom.
Curiosity turns into a habit when you repeat it. For about 35 years, he has met a new person every two weeks.
Meeting people from many different fields, such as science, medicine, politics, religion, and art, gives your curiosity wide range.
Acting on curiosity expands your world, both physically and mentally, and creates opportunities you never knew could exist.

1-sjUoGO250.summary: Deliberate practice is mindful, structured learning by doing, and it works best when you break skills into parts, go slowly, stay focused, track progress, repeat often, and use a coach.

points.text: Deliberate practice is mindful, highly structured learning by doing, using ongoing experimentation to reach mastery and eventually full automaticity of one specific skill.
List every element needed for success, then drill each one deliberately, one after another, such as tennis serves first and leg work later.
Plan your routine in a notebook, then after each session write what worked and what didn't, so you can experiment with better ways to reach your goals.
Practice slowly and correctly to build muscle memory. Moving too fast risks learning wrong skills, so raise speed gradually.
Deliberate practice is mentally hard, so keep sessions short enough to stay focused, such as 15 minutes for younger people and up to 60 for older ones.
Cut wasted time so more of it goes to real practice, like coach Wooden having players practice putting on socks and shoes quickly.
Measure progress in very small units, like milliseconds or milligrams. Smaller data points show progress faster and keep you motivated.
Great performances come from hidden hard work, so to become as good as top performers, study how they practice rather than watching them perform.
Mastery comes from huge numbers of repetitions: cigar makers got faster from 25 seconds to 8 seconds per cigar after a million repetitions.
A steady daily routine drives mastery; beginners can start with 15 minutes a day and slowly lengthen sessions. A coach shows your potential and guides you.

0af00UcTO-c.summary: Good ideas rarely come from lone eureka moments; they grow from connected networks of people and half-formed hunches that mix in open, varied environments.

points.text: Innovation thrives in spaces where people from different backgrounds and fields meet and share, like English coffeehouses, where ideas could combine.
Words like flash, epiphany and light bulb wrongly suggest an idea is a single thing that appears in one moment.
An idea is a network: a new pattern of neurons firing together in your brain that has never formed before. The outside world's networks mimic this.
Breakthroughs are usually cobbled together from nearby parts and other people's ideas, like an incubator built from car parts, rather than being brand-new inventions.
Kevin Dunbar's videotapes showed most lab breakthroughs came at group meetings where people shared data and mistakes, not alone at the microscope.
A "liquid network" is an environment where many different ideas and backgrounds jostle and bounce off each other, which leads to innovation.
The "slow hunch": many great ideas linger for years in the back of the mind before they become clear, as Darwin's notebooks showed.
Organizations should protect time for hunches to develop and let them connect with others' hunches, since two half-ideas can become something bigger.
Value connecting ideas as much as protecting them; the GPS story shows how a side hunch shared among colleagues grew in unplanned directions.
Open innovative systems, built right, lead to directions their creators never imagined. Chance favors the connected mind.

Of8VjHptafg.summary: You can learn faster by revising on a schedule, using active methods, focusing without distractions, understanding instead of memorizing, using several senses, resting well, and matching your dominant learning style.

points.text: The forgetting curve: after a week, people remember only about 15% of what they tried to memorize. Revising on days 1, 2, 3 and 4 raises retention to about 90%.
Active recall means actively doing something with what you learn: writing it, teaching it, repeating it aloud, or making flash cards with short notes to review on later days.
For skills like coding or design, you must actually do the work yourself. Just watching or reading will not make it stick in your mind.
Study in a distraction-free space: keep your desk clutter-free, put your phone away, and play only instrumental music, because lyrics pull your brain's attention.
Mnemonics are shortcuts for remembering things, like using the first letters of a sentence to recall the planets. Your brain handles patterns better.
Visualizing information as an image, pattern or story helps you remember it better, because imagery memory is stronger than verbal or auditory memory. You need not draw it.
A tired mind and body cannot absorb new information well, which makes forgetting worse. Rest properly, including short power naps of about 15 minutes.
Using more senses helps: read, speak, listen and record yourself. Asking more questions also builds understanding, taking you back to first principles instead of rote learning.

Dor28JxoHYY.summary: Build a 'second brain' with three steps, capture, connect, and create, so information you take in stays retrievable and turns into something new.

points.text: The fear of forgetting what you read or learn can be solved by building a 'second brain' that stores information for you, based on Tiago Forte's course.
The second brain method has three steps: capture, connect, and create.
Capture means saving the most important information from whatever you read or watch, for example by highlighting on a Kindle instead of using a physical highlighter.
Notes apps let you capture articles, tweets and links from anywhere in daily life, not just books.
Capture everything in one central place, because the brain stores and finds information best when it is not scattered across notebooks, cupboards and memory.
Connect means organising what you captured by tagging or classifying it, so one item can belong to several groups, like a quote that is also inspiration.
Grouping items into 'worlds' like quotes, jokes, personal finance or movies lets you instantly retrieve anything later, because each item is connected to others.
Categorising and tagging your own content, such as videos by topic, lets you find all items of one kind with a single click.
Create means using what you captured and connected to make something new. Reading a book is pointless if you learn nothing and do nothing with it.
Great creation comes from steady discipline, and connected ideas in your head make it possible. Regular use makes the second brain work with your original brain.

f7V76Ky-_v8.summary: Digital distraction comes from engineered apps that act like mild addictions, and cutting them out, keeping the phone away, and avoiding task switching lets you get far more deep work done.

points.text: Without social media, the internet becomes boring, so little tempts you away from work. Setting up your life with little of interest online protects focus.
Fear of missing something bad, like an emergency, drives phone checking. But people lived fine for generations being out of touch for hours.
The uneasy feeling when a phone dies can be seen as a moderate behavioral addiction, like a gambler feeling not themselves away from the game.
Apps are engineered to hit our alert systems, building dopamine feedback loops of anticipation and reward. When you can't check, the blocked dopamine response feels uncomfortable.
Phones and social media have real benefits, but the balance is off, like a bar with drinks too potent, making them hard to navigate.
People who cut back on these tools usually don't report losing mental sharpness or missing out. They describe coming out of a fog.
Keeping the phone out of the room lets you get much more work done. Handing it to someone else can enforce this.
Focused brainpower is limited to a few good hours a day, but prioritizing it and avoiding the phone lets results pile up over time.
Phones cost more than the time spent on them, because they trigger task switching, an expensive, slow, energy-consuming operation for the brain.

wtl5UrrgU8c.summary: Great feedback works with the brain by following a four-part formula: a micro-yes question, a specific data point, an impact statement, and a closing question, plus regularly asking for feedback.

points.text: Most feedback is not brain-friendly: being too soft leaves the brain confused, while being too direct makes the brain sense a social threat and turn defensive.
The amygdala constantly scans for social threat, so a threatening message pushes people to get defensive or retreat, and the giver then gets flustered too.
Step one, the micro-yes: start with a short question that signals feedback is coming, such as asking whether the person has five minutes to talk.
The micro-yes paces the conversation and gives the listener a moment of buy-in and a feeling of autonomy, because they can say yes or no.
Step two, the data point: state exactly what you saw or heard, using objective words and avoiding blur words that mean different things to different people.
Turn vague labels into observable facts. Instead of "you aren't reliable," say you promised an email by 11 and haven't received it. Positive feedback needs specifics too.
Step three, the impact statement: explain how the data point affected you, which gives the brain the purpose and logic it craves.
Step four, end with a question such as "How do you see it?" This builds commitment rather than compliance and turns a monologue into joint problem-solving.
Don't wait for feedback to be pushed to you; actively ask for it, called pulling feedback, which shows you are a continual learner and puts the power in your hands.

CPAhCOMhJds.summary: Choose a career by finding what overlaps between what you're good at, what you enjoy, and what the world needs, while a job covers your basic expenses.

points.text: Choosing a career is hard: parents push a few fixed options, the world offers too many, and most people don't yet know themselves well enough.
Step one: write a list of everything you are good at, such as writing, talking to friends, planning, singing or studying.
Step two: ask how much joy each skill gives you. Being good at something doesn't mean you enjoy doing it, and it can drain you.
The overlap of what you are good at and what makes you happy to do is the starting point for a career.
Step three: ask whether that skill and passion can be turned into something other people need.
A passion often must be reshaped to fit a need. The world doesn't need people who just read books, but it needs book reviewers and recommenders.
Where good at, enjoy and world needs overlap, you get a vision of what your career could be.
Once you have that idea, study how the best people in that field do it in the real world.
Don't pressure your passion to pay the bills right away. Let a job cover basic needs, and spend your spare time building the passion.

QPnPqNPHUEI.summary: Beginners' common first-job mistakes, such as staying passive, not asking for feedback, and not sharing updates, can be fixed by taking responsibility and learning from mistakes quickly.

points.text: A company hires you for the value your work creates, not just to get tasks finished quickly, so speed alone is the wrong goal.
Being smart does not matter if your manager cannot trust you, so trust is the most important thing to build.
Getting feedback is your own responsibility. If you want it, you have to ask your manager instead of waiting for it.
You should get to know people in other departments, because without understanding their point of view you cannot do your own work well.
Nobody can read your mind, so when a plan changes or you do something new, tell people through your actions and updates.
Working hard does not guarantee a promotion. Ask the company what you need to do to get promoted.
Salary is paid for the work you do for the company, not based on how much you want.
Instead of just complaining about management, try to understand the thinking behind their decisions.
Outcome is the result your work causes, while output is only the task you were told to do. Focus on outcomes.

D8Gc6_S6i0k.summary: Anxiety is often a smokescreen for deeper, more painful feelings, so asking what you would be thinking about without it can reveal what you are avoiding.

points.text: Anxious thoughts become repetitive and stuck, circling again and again around the same worry, such as whether the door is locked.
Anxiety is all-consuming: it takes over the mind, resists being questioned, and leaves us unable to think about anything except our fear.
Anxiety is frequently a smokescreen, hiding something other than what we consciously think is worrying us.
We may choose to feel anxious to avoid confronting things that are more painful or awkward, because fretting is easier than knowing ourselves.
A small worry can stand in for a bigger issue: airport anxiety may hide doubts about a holiday or marriage, and money worries may hide emotional confusion.
It is better to find the root cause of our troubles than to fill our minds with diversionary panic.
The key question to ask: if your mind weren't filled with these anxious thoughts, what might you have to think about right now?
The question can unlock insight, revealing feelings like sadness, loneliness, anger at a partner, or abandonment, which we should then process.
Some anxieties are about real worries, but a large class exists only to distract us from understanding important parts of ourselves.
If we must suffer, we should suffer for the right reasons, trading anxiety for facing the real complexity of our lives.

s2AUI-7GRJc.summary: Our constant worries about the future are often echoes of unprocessed childhood trauma, and seeing this lets us respond as capable adults rather than frightened children.

points.text: Instead of arguing against each worry one by one, it can help to look at the overall place worry holds in our lives.
Winnicott's idea: the catastrophe we fear will happen has in fact already happened, so the disaster we dread is behind us, not ahead.
We confuse past and present because childhood trauma was never properly processed, so it haunts us in adulthood like the dead who were never adequately buried and mourned.
Adult fears often repeat childhood experiences, such as panicking about humiliation or abandonment even when our partner or situation gives no real reason.
Seeing worries as legacies of childhood lets us replace dread with sadness and feel sorry for our younger selves instead of panicking about our future.
Well-parented people inherit good responses to crisis: they reach out, seek help, and take only fitting responsibility.
Without that guidance, we react to trouble like frightened children, using childlike tools such as overeating, going silent or screaming, and we lose perspective.
Reminding ourselves that we are adults means we need not be as afraid or powerless as we were as children; we can protest, argue our case and rebuild.
We can reduce risk by working on our attitude to risk, not by removing all risk from the world.
We will still worry often, but knowing the childhood roots makes us less fragile and less convinced that total catastrophe is coming.

kgVbCQZVWWw.summary: No thought is inherently negative; the real problem is thoughts running unconsciously, and the fix is to stop identifying with what you are not rather than fight your thoughts.

points.text: A thought is just a thought. If you understand this, it has no power over you; if you treat it as truth, it can destroy you.
You create your own thoughts, so you are responsible for them and can choose what to produce.
Thinking means running your thought process consciously. Thoughts flowing on their own all the time are like mental diarrhea.
The real negativity is that thoughts run unconsciously, not what the thoughts are about. Devil's thoughts versus God's thoughts is not the distinction.
Fighting thoughts you label negative ruins people, because they keep creating thoughts and then fighting them.
Fighting something you created yourself is a loss even if you win. You should create thoughts by your own will.
There are no positive or negative thoughts, only conscious thoughts or mental diarrhea.
To treat diarrhea, first stop the bad food. Whatever the cause, stop it first, before any other cure.
The bad food is identifying yourself with something you are not. While you do this, the mind will not stop, whatever mantra or god you try.

A7RWzJZY160.summary: Fear, anger and joy are all produced by your own mind, so instead of fighting them you must take charge of your mind and choose what it produces.

points.text: You don't need to go beyond fear, anger or jealousy; you only need to stop producing them.
Fear and anger are products of the mind, which happens when you haven't taken charge of it.
The mind can produce anything: joy, anxiety, restlessness, peace, agony or ecstasy.
People end up with unwanted states only because they don't know how to handle their mind.
Like a computer, the mind must be learned; not knowing where the keyboard is means pressing wrong buttons and getting chaos.
Your mind can become a miracle or a machine that produces suffering; the result depends on how you run it.
Stop producing suffering and start producing joy, since joy is what the human mind is capable of.
Pressing the wrong button and holding it makes suffering grow, so you must know which button to press and which to avoid.
Only by taking charge of your body, mind and energy yourself, not by wishing for a good result, will good things happen to you.

p7HKvqRI_Bo.summary: The stock market lets companies raise money from investors who buy ownership shares, with stock prices rising and falling as supply, demand, and investor confidence shift.

points.text: Companies can raise money by selling shares to investors, who receive a share of the profits in return. The Dutch East India Company did this to fund its ships.
A company launches on the public market through an initial public offering (IPO), first sponsored by big investors who think the company is a good idea.
Buying a stock makes an investor a partial owner of the business, and the money they put in helps the company grow.
When more people want a stock, its price rises. That raises the value of shares already owned and helps the company fund new projects.
If investors expect a stock to lose value, they sell it. Falling demand pushes the price and the company's market value down, which can cause big losses.
Many factors move supply and demand, including material prices, technology, labor costs, leadership changes, bad publicity, new laws, and investors' personal reasons for selling.
Appearing to lose value can drive investors away, and losing investors causes real loss of value. Human confidence can trigger booms or financial crises.
Because the market is so unpredictable, most professionals recommend reliable long-term investing over trying to make quick cash.
Thanks to the Internet, everyday people can buy stocks in much the same ways as large investors, supporting businesses they believe in and pursuing financial goals.

XNu5ppFZbHo.summary: A dollar's value comes from how much currency exists compared to goods and services, so the independent Fed carefully controls the money supply to keep inflation small and steady.

points.text: Government printing and designating a bill as official currency only makes it legal; its value depends on how many or few bills are in circulation.
Fiat money is currency not linked to any external resource like gold; government policy alone decides how much gets printed. The US dollar became fiat money in 1971.
An independent Federal Reserve, not the executive, legislative or judicial branch, sets monetary policy, so it is shielded from day-to-day politics.
Currency exists to be exchanged for goods and services, so printing unlimited money would make bills worthless.
Inflation happens when currency grows faster than goods and services, so each bill buys less than before.
Deflation happens when goods and services grow while the money supply stays the same, so each dollar becomes worth more.
Too much inflation makes people spend or hoard right away, which raises prices, causes shortages and creates even more inflation.
Deflation makes people hold onto money, so spending and business profits fall, unemployment rises, and the economy keeps shrinking.
Most economists say a small, consistent amount of inflation is needed to encourage economic growth, even though too much of either inflation or deflation is dangerous.
The Fed uses economic data, like past inflation, international trends and unemployment, to get the money supply just right for growth and jobs without disruptive inflation.

45ijJXd2YYE.summary: National income is understood through four measures: GDP, GNP, NDP and NNP, which differ by whether they count income earned abroad and whether they subtract depreciation.

points.text: GDP is the total value of all goods and services produced inside a country in one year.
GDP is calculated from four parts: consumption (C), investment (I), government spending (G), and net exports (exports minus imports): GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).
GDP at market price includes indirect taxes and subtracts subsidies, while GDP at factor cost does not include these.
GNP counts income earned by a country's own people anywhere in the world, not just production inside the country.
An American working in India and sending salary home counts in India's GDP but is subtracted from India's GNP.
GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA). If NFIA is positive, GNP exceeds GDP; if negative, GNP is lower.
Depreciation is machines, buildings and equipment losing value as they age. NDP = GDP − depreciation, showing real production without those losses.
NNP = GNP − depreciation. NNP at factor cost is called national income, while NNP at market price includes indirect taxes and subsidies.
Governments focus on GDP growth, but NNP at factor cost (national income) matters most for actual income and standard of living.

HBR1yemoDCs.summary: Discipline comes from how your brain's decision-making and habit systems work, so you build it by shaping your environment, cutting choices, forming habits, and choosing your people.

points.text: The prefrontal cortex handles impulse control and long-term planning, like deciding on future goals or saying no to chocolate.
The striatum forms habits and takes over routine daily decisions, like a vice president handling small choices so the prefrontal cortex doesn't have to.
Discipline starts as an effortful prefrontal cortex decision, then becomes a habit in the striatum, which takes far less effort.
Willpower is limited. The amygdala keeps interrupting with temptations, and spending willpower on small decisions leaves less for big ones, as with impulse buys at supermarket checkouts.
Everything around you acts as a cue that shapes your thinking, so change your environment, such as laying out gym clothes or moving your phone away.
Reduce friction by simplifying important areas of life with fewer choices, like a similar breakfast and workout routine, so your prefrontal cortex tires less.
Build habits with four laws: make it obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying. Each works on the brain differently, through cues, dopamine, lower friction, and reinforcement.
The people around you shape your thoughts and actions, so surround yourself with people passionate about your goal, plus people who help you stay calm.
Discipline is an input your environment gives you, not an output you bring to it. Trying to be disciplined in a chaotic environment makes life harder.

arj7oStGLkU.summary: Procrastinators have an Instant Gratification Monkey that overrides the Rational Decision-Maker until the Panic Monster appears, and deadline-free areas of life are where procrastination does the most lasting harm.

points.text: A procrastinator's brain has a Rational Decision-Maker like everyone else's, but also an Instant Gratification Monkey that competes for control.
The Monkey lives only in the present, with no memory of the past or knowledge of the future, and cares only about what is easy and fun.
The Rational Decision-Maker can visualize the future, see the big picture and make long-term plans, so it wants us to do whatever makes sense right now.
Easy and fun sometimes matches what makes sense, like dinner or earned leisure. When hard work makes more sense, the two conflict, and the procrastinator's Monkey wins.
The Dark Playground is leisure at the wrong time. It isn't truly fun because it is unearned, and it fills with guilt, dread, anxiety and self-hatred.
With deadlines, procrastination's damage stays short-term because the Panic Monster steps in. The procrastinator's system is ugly, but it works.

Without deadlines, such as starting a creative career, exercising, or fixing relationships, the Panic Monster never shows up, so procrastination goes on indefinitely and can cause long-term unhappiness and regret.
Long-term procrastination makes people feel like spectators in their own lives. The pain is not failing to reach dreams but never starting to chase them.
Everyone procrastinates on something, so everyone should stay aware of the Monkey and look at what they're putting off, since a life has a limited number of weeks.

v-t1Z5-oPtU.summary: Stress is a physical response that helps briefly but, when chronic, damages the heart, gut, weight, immune system and cells; how you respond to it matters.

points.text: Stress is not just a feeling; it is a hardwired physical response that travels through your whole body. Briefly it helps, but too often or too long it harms.
The adrenal gland releases stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline, norepinephrine) that travel in the blood to reach the blood vessels and heart.
Adrenaline speeds up the heartbeat and raises blood pressure, which over time causes hypertension.
Cortisol can stop the inner lining of blood vessels working normally, an early step toward cholesterol plaque in arteries, raising heart attack and stroke risk.
The brain passes stress to the gut's nervous system, disturbing food movement, causing irritable bowel syndrome and heartburn, and changing gut bacteria.
Cortisol raises appetite and cravings for comfort foods, and encourages deep belly fat, which releases hormones and cytokines that raise risk of heart disease and insulin resistance.
Stress hormones first help immune cells fight invaders and heal, but chronic stress weakens some immune cells, causing more infections and slower healing.
Chronic stress is linked to shorter telomeres, the chromosome end caps that shorten with each cell division; when too short, the cell dies.
Chronic stress can also cause acne, hair loss, headaches, muscle tension, fatigue, poor concentration and irritability.
Stress is unavoidable, but seeing situations as challenges you can master rather than insurmountable threats helps you perform better now and stay healthier long term.

BHY0FxzoKZE.summary: Regular physical activity boosts your brain right away, builds lasting improvements in memory, focus and mood, and helps protect the brain from age-related disease.

points.text: The prefrontal cortex, behind the forehead, handles decision-making, focus, attention and personality. The hippocampus, deep in the temporal lobe, forms and keeps long-term memories for facts and events.
Regular exercise made the speaker feel more energetic and happier, and she noticed she could focus longer and remember better. This suggested exercise was changing her brain.
A single workout has immediate effects: it raises the neurotransmitters dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline, which lifts your mood right afterward.
One workout also improves your ability to shift and focus attention for at least two hours, and it speeds up your reaction times.
Immediate effects are temporary. Lasting benefits need a changed routine that raises your cardiorespiratory fitness, because long-term exercise changes the brain's anatomy, physiology and function.
Long-term exercise creates new brain cells in the hippocampus, increasing its volume and improving long-term memory.
Long-term exercise also improves attention, which depends on the prefrontal cortex, and keeps the good-mood neurotransmitters raised for a long time.
A good minimum is aerobic exercise that raises your heart rate, at least 30 minutes, three to four times a week. Walking, taking stairs or power-vacuuming can count.

1DRq8N7SpYc.summary: A SIP invests a fixed amount every month regardless of market moves, which builds wealth steadily with little risk, and choosing a direct plan keeps more of your money.

points.text: A SIP (systematic investment plan) means investing money regularly, every month, instead of all at once.
A mutual fund unit has a price called NAV (net asset value). When the NAV rises, the value of your investment rises with it.
With a SIP you invest on the same date each month and do not worry about whether the market is up or down.
Example: putting ₹5,000 a month into one fund from 2013 to 2021 turned about ₹4.9 lakh invested into about ₹11.6 lakh.
Converted to a yearly figure, that SIP earned roughly 11% a year on average over 8 years, with no extra risk taken.
Expense ratio is the percentage of your money the fund deducts each year for its costs, so only the rest gets invested.
A regular plan includes an agent's commission inside the expense ratio, so it costs more than a direct plan. Moving regular funds to direct is worthwhile.
Switching from regular to direct can trigger an exit load and short-term capital gains tax (15%) if you sell within a year, so time it carefully.
Investing a lump sum all at once is risky because bad timing can hurt. A lump sum put in before the 2020 crash lost about 20%.
For a lump sum, park it in a debt fund and move a fixed amount into a SIP every month, so you avoid timing the market.

9MdbLP6hQ7E.summary: A budget is a plan for dividing limited money so you spend only what you decided on each thing, which teaches the value of spending wisely.

points.text: To make a budget, first find the prices of everything needed, and don't leave costs until the last moment.
A budget is a way of dividing your money so that you spend only the amount you decided for each purpose.
Budgeting is like splitting three chips packets across lunch, snack and dinner instead of eating them all at once; the same idea applies to money.
You should know when and how to spend your money, not spend it all at once.
Split the money into categories, such as sweets, vegetables and flowers, then research prices for each category.
Compare prices across several shops before choosing, and pick based on price and quality, such as the cheapest flower shop or the best-tasting sweets.
Extra effort, like noting each item's price in every shop, can reveal savings and free extras that a quick check would miss.
Everyone has limited money, so it must be spent thoughtfully; careless spending leaves nothing behind.
Children can practise this too: demanding unneeded toys or clothes from parents upsets their budget, so pause and think about the money's value first.
Spending on unnecessary things leaves less money for necessary ones, so think many times before buying and spend only when truly needed.

erfgEHHfFkU.summary: Emotional intelligence has four learnable domains (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management) that together make up effective leadership and outstanding performance.

points.text: Emotional intelligence combines self-awareness, managing your emotions, tuning into others through empathy, and using all this to build effective relationships. Outstanding leaders and performers score high in it.
Unlike IQ, which barely changes, emotional intelligence can be learned at any age.
Self-awareness means knowing what you feel and how that feeling shapes your perceptions, thoughts, and urge to act. Because emotion directs attention, this matters for how you experience each moment.
Self-awareness is the least visible domain but the foundation: people low in it struggle to build other emotional skills, while people high in it can often excel across the board.
Self-management has four parts: handling upsetting emotions, marshaling positive emotions, staying agile with a growth mindset, and keeping focus on your goal despite distractions.
Social awareness centers on empathy, or tuning in to the people around you, and it has three parts.
Cognitive empathy is understanding how another person sees the situation, including the language they use to explain it. This lets you phrase messages so they land.
Emotional empathy is the brain automatically locking onto another person's actions, intentions, and feelings, so you feel what they feel and stay emotionally on the same page.
Empathic concern is caring: knowing what someone thinks and feels and also showing you care about them. It builds strong trust and rapport between leaders and their people.
Relationship management is using your skills to guide, influence, inspire, work in teams, handle conflict calmly, and coach others to become future leaders.

NdI6jMja3Bs.summary: Emotional intelligence grows by understanding why you act, listening to understand, reading body language, pausing before reacting to emotions, staying positive, welcoming feedback, and being grateful.

points.text: Self-awareness means knowing why you do things. Asking yourself "why" five times in a row gets past surface answers to your real reason.
Most people listen only to prepare their reply. An effective listener tries to understand the other person, and understanding matters more than answering.
Most communication is not words. Body, hands, face and voice carry about 70 to 75 percent, so working on nonverbal signals builds emotional intelligence.
Notice other people's nonverbal emotions too. If their words and their face disagree, they may not be telling the truth.
You cannot stop feeling emotions because you are human. Emotionally intelligent people don't claim to control emotions; they know what they feel and why.
You can't control the emotion, but your reaction is your choice: react instantly, or take time, be aware of the feeling, and respond thoughtfully.
Replies written in high emotion achieve nothing. They turn into defending yourself and blaming the other person, creating a setting where healthy conversation is impossible.
Emotionally intelligent people stay positive: they fix problems instead of complaining, and know they can change difficulties. Much of life, like friends, work and news, is your choice.
Emotionally intelligent people ask for feedback. Hearing where you are wrong may hurt in one person's eyes, but fixing it raises you in everyone else's.
Emotionally intelligent people are grateful for their family, friends, love and opportunities. They see other people as help or inspiration, not as rivals.
